::: {.callout-note}
## Attribution

The π example and the sequence of cases follow George G. Vega Yon's workshop *HPC with Slurm, R and the slurmR package* (<https://github.com/USCbiostats/slurmr-workshop>{target="_blank"}), adapted to CHPC and to plain Slurm (no slurmR package). The coding-agent setup follows CHPC's session *Coding Agents at CHPC* (November 10).
:::

## Learning goals

- Run the same R simulation serially, on several cores, and as a Slurm job array, and get **exactly the same answer** every time.
- Ask Slurm for cores and make R use exactly those cores.
- Split a simulation across array tasks and combine the results with a dependent job.
- Use a coding agent on CHPC to write and debug Slurm jobs, and check its work against a known answer.
- Measure speedup and explain why it is less than the number of cores.

## Lab description

Work in **pairs**. Each of you needs a CHPC account; you can share one screen when it helps. Keep a record of **every prompt you send to Codex and a short note on what came back**, as in all our labs; this is part of the deliverable.

Submit a single Quarto document (`lab11.qmd`), its rendered HTML, your scripts, and `timings.csv` in a new folder `lab11/` of your class repository by Sunday, as usual.

| When | What | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Before class | [Checklist](#before-class) | 10 min |
| In class | [Hands-on 1](#hands-on-1): cases 1 and 2 by hand | 20 min |
| In class | [Hands-on 2](#hands-on-2): Codex writes the job array | 35 min |
| At home | [Homework](#homework): spot the bug, scaling report, submit | 50 min |

**The known answers.** Every correct version of the simulation prints these values (12 digits):

| Size (`nsims`, `n`) | Used for | π̂ |
|---|---|---|
| 100, 10,000 | tiny tests | 3.140208000000 |
| 10,000, 10,000 (default) | quick runs, the buggy script | 3.141755000000 |
| 10,000, 100,000 | timings on CHPC | 3.141601060000 |

## Before class (10 minutes) {#before-class}

1. **Get the scripts on CHPC.** Log in to [Open OnDemand](https://ondemand.chpc.utah.edu){target="_blank"} and start an interactive **desktop** session (Codex sign-in needs a browser on the same machine). In the desktop, open a terminal and run:

    ```bash
    git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/UofUEpiBio/PHS7045-advanced-programming.git ~/phs7045-course
    mkdir -p ~/lab11
    cp -r ~/phs7045-course/11-simpi/scripts/. ~/lab11/
    cd ~/lab11 && ls
    ```

    You should see `simpi.R`, the `0*-*.R` and `0*-*.slurm` files, `AGENTS.md`, and a `buggy/` folder.

2. **Sign in to Codex.**

    ```bash
    module load codex
    cd ~/lab11
    codex
    ```

    Sign in with your university account in the browser window that opens. Then ask Codex: *"Which rules apply in this folder?"* It should list the rules from `AGENTS.md`. Exit Codex.

3. **If sign-in fails**, try `module load codex_CHPC_local_model` (a CHPC-hosted model, no sign-in needed) and tell us at the start of class.

4. **On your laptop**, create the folder `lab11/` in your class repository, copy the same scripts into it (from the course repository, or with `scp -r <uid>@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu:~/lab11/ .`), and create `lab11.qmd`.

## Hands-on 1: cases 1 and 2 by hand (20 minutes) {#hands-on-1}

**No coding agents in this part.** You learn the mechanics by doing them yourself.

### 1a. On your laptop (8 minutes)

In the `lab11/` folder on your laptop, run:

```bash
Rscript 01-sapply.R                       # default size
Rscript 01-sapply.R 10000 100000          # timing size, about 30 s
Rscript 02-mclapply.R 10000 100000 4      # same, on 4 cores
```

Windows users: `02-mclapply.R` switches to a socket cluster automatically.

Create `timings.csv` with this content and fill in the first two rows from the output (`elapsed` and `pi-hat`):

```default
where,tasks,cores_per_task,total_cores,elapsed_sec,pi_hat
laptop,1,1,1,,
laptop,1,4,4,,
chpc,1,4,4,,
chpc,4,4,16,,
```

In `lab11.qmd`, answer:

a. Does the default run print the known answer? Do the two timing runs print the **same** π̂?

b. What speedup $S_4 = T_1 / T_4$ do you get? Why is it less than 4?

### 1b. On CHPC (12 minutes)

In the OnDemand terminal, in `~/lab11`:

```bash
cat 00-hello-world.slurm          # read it first
sbatch 00-hello-world.slurm
squeue --me                       # is it pending (PD) or running (R)?
cat hello-world-*.out             # once it has finished
```

Now read `02-mclapply.slurm` and `02-mclapply.R`, then submit it and **move on**; it runs in the background:

```bash
sbatch 02-mclapply.slurm          # note the job ID
```

When it is done, read its log (`02-mclapply-<jobid>.out`) and save its accounting record for the report:

```bash
sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,Start,End,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,NodeList,State --parsable2 > sacct-02-mclapply.txt
```

In `lab11.qmd`, answer:

c. Which node ran your hello-world job? Was it a login node?

d. How does `02-mclapply.R` know how many cores it may use? What would go wrong with `mc.cores = parallel::detectCores()` on CHPC?

e. Does the CHPC run print the same π̂ as your laptop?

## Hands-on 2: Codex writes the job array (35 minutes) {#hands-on-2}

Now we go to many nodes: **4 array tasks × 4 cores**, plus a job that combines the results. This time Codex writes the code; you write the specification, test the code, and submit it.

### 2a. Write the spec first (5 minutes)

Copy this into `lab11.qmd` and fill in the blanks **before** you prompt Codex:

```default
Goal: run the pi simulation (nsims = 10000, n = 100000) as a Slurm job array
with 4 tasks and 4 cores per task, reusing simpi.R, and combine the results
in a second job.

Acceptance tests (and how I will check each one):
1. The combined pi-hat is ______________ to all 12 digits.
   Check: ____________________________________________
2. Every task records the node it ran on.
   Check: ____________________________________________
3. Every task writes its own file; after the run there are exactly ___ files.
   Check: ____________________________________________
4. The combining job starts only after all tasks finished successfully.
   Check: ____________________________________________
```

### 2b. Plan, then build (15 minutes)

Start Codex in `~/lab11` (`module load codex`, then `codex`). Paste this prompt, adding your four tests where indicated:

```{.default}
P1
Read @simpi.R, @02-mclapply.R, @02-mclapply.slurm and AGENTS.md.
I want to run the same pi simulation (nsims = 10000, n = 100000) as a Slurm
job array with 4 tasks and 4 cores per task, plus a second job that combines
the results. My acceptance tests are:
[paste your four tests here]
Do not write any files yet. Propose a plan: which files you will create, how
the replicates are split across tasks, what each task saves, and the exact
commands I should run to test it on a tiny problem and to submit it.
```

Read the plan. Does it reuse `make_seeds()` and `simpi()` unchanged? Does it give each task its own output file? Ask for changes if needed, then:

```{.default}
P2
The plan looks good. Write 03-array.R, 03-array.slurm, 04-aggregate.R and
04-aggregate.slurm. Use the same account and partition as 02-mclapply.slurm.
```

### 2c. Test on a tiny problem, then submit (10 minutes)

Test first, on the login node, with a **tiny** size (allowed by our `AGENTS.md`). Pretend to be Slurm by setting the variables yourself:

```bash
for a in 1 2 3 4; do
  SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=$a SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT=4 SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK=1 \
    Rscript 03-array.R 100 10000
done
Rscript 04-aggregate.R 100 10000     # must print 3.140208000000
bash -n 03-array.slurm && bash -n 04-aggregate.slurm && echo "syntax OK"
```

(If Codex's scripts take the size in a different way, adapt the commands.) When the tiny test passes, clean up its results (`mv results results-tiny`) and **submit it yourself**:

```bash
jid=$(sbatch --parsable 03-array.slurm)
echo "array job ID: $jid"        # write it down; you need it for sacct
sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid 04-aggregate.slurm
squeue --me
```

### 2d. Check (5 minutes)

When both jobs are done, go through your four acceptance tests and mark each one passed or failed. Save the accounting record of the array:

```bash
sacct -j <array job ID> --format=JobID,JobName,Start,End,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,NodeList,State --parsable2 > sacct-03-array.txt
```

In `lab11.qmd`, answer:

f. Which tests passed on the first try? What did you have to correct, and would you have noticed without the known answer?

g. On how many distinct nodes did your 4 tasks run? Why might they all end up on the same node?

## Homework (about 50 minutes) {#homework}

### H1. Spot the bug (15 minutes)

The folder `buggy/` has a colleague's version of case 2: `05-buggy.R` and `05-buggy.slurm`. It has **three** problems.

a. **By hand first (5 minutes).** Read both files without running anything and list every problem you see.

b. **Run it.** `cd ~/lab11/buggy && sbatch 05-buggy.slurm`. What happens?

c. **Ask Codex** (CHPC's `job-triage` skill should kick in):

    ```{.default}
    P3
    My job script @buggy/05-buggy.slurm does not run, and I suspect that
    @buggy/05-buggy.R has problems too. Diagnose both files. Do not change
    anything yet: list each problem, how you found it, and how to fix it.
    ```

d. Fix the Slurm problem only, submit again, and compare the printed π̂ with the known answer for this size (10,000 × 10,000: 3.141755000000). Submit it a second time. Is the result the same?

e. Fill in this table in `lab11.qmd`:

    | Problem | Found by me? | Found by Codex? | How does it show up? (error / wrong answer / nothing visible) |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | | | | |
    | | | | |
    | | | | |

    Which of the problems would you have caught **without** the known answer?

### H2. Scaling report (30 minutes)

Fill in the last two rows of `timings.csv` from `sacct-02-mclapply.txt` and `sacct-03-array.txt`. For the array, the wall time is from the start of the first task to the end of the last one. Codex can help:

```{.default}
P4
Read @sacct-02-mclapply.txt and @sacct-03-array.txt. For each job, report
the wall time (for the array: from the first task's start to the last task's
end), the allocated cores, and the CPU efficiency (TotalCPU divided by
Elapsed x AllocCPUS). Then write an R script scaling.R that reads
@timings.csv, adds speedup (relative to the laptop with 1 core) and
efficiency columns, and plots speedup against total cores with a dashed
line for perfect scaling.
```

Then:

a. **Check one number yourself.** Pick one row of the table and recompute its wall time and efficiency by hand from the raw `sacct` file. Does it match what Codex reported?

b. Include the table and the plot in `lab11.qmd` (run `scaling.R` from a chunk).

c. Answer, in a few sentences each:

    1. Why is the speedup on 16 cores less than 16? Name at least two causes you can see in your data.
    2. Suppose each replicate took a hundredth of a second and you ran 1,000 array tasks. What would dominate the wall time?
    3. How would you structure the simulation of your final project the same way (replicates, one seed per replicate, one output file per task)?

### H3. Submit (5 minutes)

Copy your CHPC files to your laptop (`scp -r <uid>@notchpeak.chpc.utah.edu:~/lab11/ .`), then push the `lab11/` folder of your class repository with:

- `lab11.qmd` and its rendered HTML, including your **prompt log** (P1--P4 and any follow-ups, with a short note on what came back),
- your spec with the acceptance tests marked passed/failed,
- Codex's `03-array.*` and `04-aggregate.*` (as corrected by you), your fixed `05-buggy.*`,
- `timings.csv`, the `sacct-*.txt` files, and `scaling.R`.
